For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let
$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
be long exact sequences in an abelian category, together with a morphism of
these sequences. If the four comparison maps at $A_{n-1},A_n,A_{n+2},A_{n+3}$
are isomorphisms, then the comparison map $A_{n+1} \to B_{n+1}$ is an
isomorphism.

Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, where $R$ is commutative unital and orientation means the supplied orientation on $N=M\setminus A$. There is a unique class
$$z\in H_n(M,A;R)$$
whose restriction at every point of $N$ is the prescribed local generator. The connecting map sends $z$ to a class $\partial z\in H_{n-1}(A;R)$ whose restrictions are local generators at every boundary point. These restrictions form the induced orientation of $A$, and $\partial z$ is its fundamental class.

The sign convention is outward-normal-first. More explicitly, in coordinates consisting of $n-1$ tangent directions followed by an inward collar coordinate, the induced boundary generator is $(-1)^n$ times the tangent generator for the corresponding product orientation. Empty boundary and dimension zero are included. No AC is used.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

derivations.claim: Enlarge the interiors of the handlebodies across a thin common collar from [F4]. These two open sets cover $Y$, retract to $U_\alpha,U_\beta$, and their intersection retracts to $\Sigma$. Mayer–Vietoris [F1] has the exact segment $$H_2(Y;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_1(U_\alpha;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(U_\beta;\mathbb Q).$$ Its first term is zero, so the second arrow is injective. Consequently the kernels of the two individual inclusion maps from the surface have zero intersection. This uses the actual rational homology hypothesis, without replacing $Y$ by a three-sphere or invoking a torsion Spin-c assertion. [F1, F4, given, construct, algebra]

For either complete attaching system write $C$ for the union of its circles. Cutting the surface along them gives a connected compact oriented surface $S$ with two boundary copies of each circle. To see connectedness from the stated disk condition, cut the handlebody along its specified disks. Its boundary is the sphere boundary of the resulting ball. Removing the interiors of the two disk faces for each compression disk leaves exactly $S$. A sphere with finitely many pairwise disjoint open disk interiors removed is connected: connect two retained points by a path on the sphere and replace every excursion through any removed disk by a boundary-circle arc; finitely many small path adjustments in the disk collars give a path avoiding their interiors. There are finitely many disk faces, and each replacement can be made for an entire excursion interval by its first and last intersection. Thus the required cut surface is connected, including the empty-system case. [F4, given, construct, algebra]

The annular-neighborhood comparison in [F2] identifies $$H_2(\Sigma,C;\mathbb Q)\cong H_2(S,\partial S;\mathbb Q).$$ Explicitly replace $C$ by disjoint thin annuli retracting onto it, using its finite smooth collars in the oriented surface; pair sequences and the five lemma preserve the relative groups. Excise smaller closed middle annuli, and retract the remaining collar pieces onto the boundary copies of the cut surface. These operations are the displayed isomorphism. The group on the right is one-dimensional on $[S,\partial S]$. Here is the needed top-degree calculation from [F3]: the local value of any relative class at an interior point is a rational multiple of the oriented local generator. Those multiples are locally constant, since restricting to a closed coordinate disk makes the class a multiple of that disk's relative orientation class. The disk relative group is $\mathbb Q$: its pair sequence and a cover of its boundary circle by two open arcs give $H_1(S^1;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$ by [F1]; both arcs are contractible, their intersection has two contractible components, and the kernel on $H_0$ is generated by their difference. Connectedness of the interior of $S$ makes all local multiples one rational number $a$. Subtracting $a[S,\partial S]$ has zero restriction at every interior point and is zero by the pointwise uniqueness in [F3]. This proves the claim, also when $S$ is closed. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

The connector from this one-dimensional relative group to $H_1(C;\mathbb Q)$ is zero. Indeed the boundary of its generator is the sum of the oriented boundary circles of $S$ by [F3]; the two copies of each cut circle map back to that circle with opposite orientations and cancel. Exactness of the pair sequence [F2] therefore makes $$H_1(C;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$$ injective. Its source has one independent rational generator for each attaching circle: finite disjoint unions split the singular chain complex, and the circle computation in step 2.1 gives one copy of $\mathbb Q$ for each circle. Thus a rational linear combination of the full oriented attaching circles which is zero in surface homology has every coefficient zero. This establishes the needed independence without an assumed symplectic basis or an integral surface intersection theorem. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Write $\partial P=c_\alpha+c_\beta$ in full-circle coefficients. This formal region chain supplies a genuine homological boundary on $\Sigma$: take relative orientation chains of its finitely many region closures, separating their corners and rounding them in small vertex disks. Paired edge contributions cancel with the prescribed coefficients; the remaining corner arcs fill in those vertex disks. The connector construction in [F2] and the orientation-boundary statement [F3] consequently give $[c_\alpha]+[c_\beta]=0$ in $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$. Each $c_\gamma$ bounds its integral combination of the specified compression disks inside $U_\gamma$. Therefore $[c_\alpha]=-[c_\beta]$ belongs to both kernels in step 1.1 and must be zero. Step 3.1 applied separately to the two complete systems makes every full-circle coefficient in $c_\alpha,c_\beta$ zero. Hence $\partial P=0$ as a region-chain boundary, not just in homology. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Across each curve edge the adjacent region coefficients of $P$ are now equal. The adjacency graph of the regions is connected. Indeed a path between two interior points on the connected surface may be altered in finitely many coordinate disks to miss the finitely many curve-intersection vertices and to cross the smooth edges transversely. One may first replace it by finitely many coordinate polygonal segments, and choose their vertices outside the finite exceptional lines and critical tangencies; in each smooth arc chart use a short transverse segment. Following this path propagates equality of the adjacent coefficients. Thus all coefficients are one integer $c$, giving $P=c[\Sigma]$. Evaluating at $z$ gives $n_z(P)=c$. If that coefficient is zero, the domain is zero, proving the admissibility assertion. For genus zero there are no attaching curves, so the same connected-surface coefficient argument applies directly. A rational homology sphere has $H_2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by definition, so it is among the stated inputs. No analytic existence, index or invariant claim entered the proof. [step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 explicitly treats the genus-zero empty attaching systems.
Step 5.1 identifies zero basepoint coefficient with c=0 and the zero domain.
Steps 1.2 and 2.1 use exactly one cut ball/connected cut surface for each complete system; the Statement retains one basepoint.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes actual complete transverse Heegaard systems; noncomplete multipointed systems are expressly excluded.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 accounts for both boundary copies of each cut circle and step 3.1 cancels their opposite orientations.
The Statement uses countable choice; the proof uses finite collars, supplied homology and localorientation uniqueness, with no fullAC surface duality theorem.
